claims.text: The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
The starting HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of 13.5%.
The baseline alloy exhibits limited strain hardening and rapid failure at high dynamic strain rates.
Controlled thermomechanical processing with minor micro-alloying can create a fine dispersion of secondary precipitates in a refined HfZrTiTa0.53 matrix.
The proposed secondary precipitates, including refractory carbides or nitrides, will be ductile.
Introducing the precipitate dispersion will engineer a dual-phase microstructure.
Nanoscale precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The precipitates will promote heterogeneous deformation and increase the density of mobile dislocations.
The precipitates will hinder shear-band propagation.
Continuous dislocation pinning and stress redistribution will enhance dynamic strain hardening during rapid deformation.
Enhanced dynamic strain hardening will retard strain localization and improve uniform plastic deformation.
The modified alloy will have yield and compressive strengths approximately 10–20% higher than the baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit greater uniform deformation and resistance to dynamic localization than the baseline.
The modified microstructure will increase impact-energy absorption.
The modified alloy will produce a slower and lower energy release under impact loading, mitigating rapid failure.
The prediction applies to adiabatic dynamic compression at approximately 10^3 s^-1.
The intervention may become less effective at very high temperatures or under different loading regimes because of thermal-stability issues.
